mainTopic: Wine and long hair for כהנים nowadays, and the days of מגילת תענית on which הספד is forbidden
overview: The amud opens by asking why, according to the רבנן, כהנים may not drink wine nowadays but may let their hair grow long (פרועי ראש). The first answer is that a drunk כהן cannot be ready quickly if the בית המקדש is rebuilt, while a haircut takes only a moment. רמי בר אבא's rule that a short nap clears wine seems to challenge this, but that rule works only for a small amount of wine. רב אשי gives a different reason: wine makes the עבודה invalid, but long hair does not. A ברייתא says both are punished by death, and the גמרא learns this for long hair from neighboring פסוקים in יחזקאל. It explains that the comparison covers only the death penalty, and that the law was an old oral tradition which יחזקאל only attached to a פסוק. The גמרא then turns to the days listed in מגילת תענית and asks why the list includes ראש חודש ניסן. The answer is that rabbinic days need a fence on the day before, while תורה days like ראש חודש do not. A similar question about the end of פסח begins, and רב פפא's answer continues on the next amud.

steps.title: If the Rabbis forbid wine nowadays, why not long hair?
steps.stepSummary: אביי's statement that כהנים today drink wine only according to רבי implies that the רבנן forbid it, which raises a question about long hair.
steps.simpleTranslation: Today's כהנים drink wine in line with רבי. That implies the רבנן forbid it! So why don't they forbid long hair too?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes אביי's statement and draws an implication from it. That implication sets up a hidden question the next step will answer: why the רבנן forbid wine nowadays but not long hair.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If only רבי allows wine today, the רבנן must still forbid it, out of concern for the future בית המקדש. The same concern should apply to פרועי ראש, since a כהן with long hair is also forbidden to serve. The גמרא does not say this question out loud, but the next step answers it.

keyTerms.meaning: By implication; from the fact that

steps.confusionAlert: The question about long hair is never written out here. The answer in the next step shows that it is the unspoken challenge.

phrases.english: It is in accordance with רבי.
phrases.notes: This ends אביי's statement from just before: the כהנים who drink wine today are relying on רבי.

phrases.english: This implies that the Rabbis forbid it!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws an implication from אביי's statement, which comes before this section
steps.kashyaTarget: The fact that the רבנן forbid wine nowadays but not long hair
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the reason is readiness for the future Temple, both disqualifications should be forbidden today.

steps.title: Wine causes a long delay, but a haircut is quick
steps.stepSummary: The reason for forbidding wine is so a fit כהן will be ready when the Temple is rebuilt. With hair, a כהן can simply cut it and go in.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the reason? The Temple may be rebuilt soon, and we will need a כהן fit to serve, and there won't be one. But here, with hair, he can cut it and go in.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why the רבנן forbid wine nowadays but not long hair.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The worry is that the בית המקדש could be rebuilt suddenly and no כהן would be ready. Wine takes a long time to wear off, so a drunk כהן could not serve right away. Long hair can be cut immediately, so there is no real delay.

keyTerms.meaning: May the Temple be rebuilt speedily

phrases.english: What is the reason?
The Temple may soon be rebuilt,
and we will need a priest fit for the service,
and there won't be one.
phrases.notes: Because they all drank wine and are not yet fit to serve.

phrases.english: Here, it is possible for him to cut his hair and enter.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the unspoken question of step 1
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinction based on how quickly the problem can be fixed
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Wine and long hair should both be forbidden nowadays
steps.terutzMaskana: Wine causes a long delay, while hair can be cut immediately, so only wine was forbidden

steps.title: Wine can also be dispelled quickly by a short nap
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the distinction: according to רמי בר אבא, a little sleep removes the effect of wine, so a drunk כהן could also be ready quickly.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, a wine-drinker too can sleep a little and go in, as רמי בר אבא said: walking a מיל, or sleeping even a little, removes the effect of wine!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the answer from step 2 by showing that wine can also be removed quickly.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 2 depended on wine causing a long delay. רמי בר אבא teaches that a short walk or a brief nap clears the wine. If so, wine is just as quick to fix as hair, and the distinction falls apart.

keyTerms.meaning: Walking a distance of a מיל

phrases.english: If so, one who drank wine too:
it is possible for him to sleep a little and enter,
in line with רמי בר אבא.
For רמי בר אבא said:
Walking a מיל, and sleeping any amount,
phrases.notes: A מיל is a fairly short walk, roughly a kilometer.

phrases.english: dispel the effect of the wine!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer of step 2
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that wine causes a long delay
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Since a brief nap removes the wine, wine is as quick to fix as hair.

steps.title: A nap only helps after a small amount of wine
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the challenge: רמי בר אבא's rule applies only to a רביעית. With more wine, walking tires him out and sleep makes him drunker.
steps.simpleTranslation: Wasn't it said about this, in the name of רב נחמן quoting רבה בר אבוה: they taught this only when he drank a רביעית. But if he drank more than a רביעית, the walk wears him out even more and the sleep makes him drunker.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the challenge of step 3 by limiting רמי בר אבא's rule, which saves the answer of step 2.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רמי בר אבא's quick fix works only for a small amount of wine. Someone who drank more cannot clear it quickly, and walking or sleeping makes it worse. So wine can still cause a long delay, and the distinction from hair stands.

keyTerms.meaning: A quarter-לוג, a small measure of liquid

steps.whatToRemember: Wine forbidden nowadays (according to the רבנן) because a drunk כהן may not be ready quickly. Long hair is not forbidden because it can be cut at once.

phrases.english: Wasn't it stated about this:

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב נַחְמָן אָמַר רַבָּה בַּר אֲבוּהּ:
phrases.english: רב נחמן said in the name of רבה בר אבוה:

phrases.aramaic: לֹא שָׁנוּ אֶלָּא בְּשֶׁשָּׁתָה שִׁיעוּר רְבִיעִית,
phrases.english: They taught this only when he drank the amount of a רביעית,
but if he drank more than a רביעית,
all the more so the walk wears him out,
and sleep makes him drunk.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the challenge of step 3
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Limits רמי בר אבא's rule so it no longer undermines step 2
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The challenge assumed the quick fix works for any amount of wine, but it works only for a רביעית

steps.title: רב אשי: wine invalidates the service, long hair does not
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי gives a different reason: wine-drinkers make the עבודה invalid, so the רבנן made a decree, but long hair does not invalidate it, so there was no decree.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי said: those who drank wine make the service invalid, so the רבנן made a decree about them. Those with long hair do not make the service invalid, so the רבנן did not make a decree about them.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי offers a different explanation for why wine is forbidden nowadays but long hair is not.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Instead of speed of repair, רב אשי looks at how serious each problem is. A כהן who drank wine makes his עבודה invalid, so the רבנן protected against it even today. A long-haired כהן's service is still valid, so no decree was needed.

phrases.english: רב אשי said:
Those who drank wine, who make the service invalid:
the Rabbis made a decree about them.
Those with long hair, who do not make the service invalid:
the Rabbis did not make a decree about them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a second answer to the question of step 1
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinction based on whether the service is invalidated
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Both wine and long hair should be forbidden nowadays
steps.terutzMaskana: Only wine, which invalidates the service, was forbidden

steps.title: A ברייתא lists both wine and long hair as punishable by death
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a ברייתא against רב אשי that lists wine-drinkers and long-haired כהנים together as punished by death.
steps.simpleTranslation: They challenged: and these are punished by death: those who drank wine, and those with long hair.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins a challenge to רב אשי by quoting a ברייתא. This sets up the next move, so the full force of the challenge has not yet been spelled out.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב אשי treated long hair as much less serious than wine. This ברייתא puts the two side by side with the same death penalty, which suggests they may be equally serious. Before pressing the point, the גמרא first asks where the long-hair penalty comes from.

keyTerms.meaning: Punished by death (at the hands of Heaven)

phrases.english: They challenged: and these are punished by death:
phrases.notes: This means death at the hands of Heaven, not by a court.

phrases.english: those who drank wine, and those with long hair.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a challenge to רב אשי's answer in step 5
steps.kashyaTarget: רב אשי's claim that long hair does not invalidate the service
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא puts long hair alongside wine with the same death penalty, suggesting they are alike.

steps.title: Where do we learn the death penalty for long hair?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא notes that the death penalty for wine is written clearly in the תורה and asks for the source for long hair.
steps.simpleTranslation: It makes sense for wine-drinkers, since it is written clearly about them: 'Drink no wine nor strong drink.' But for those with long hair, where do we learn it?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pauses the challenge to ask for the source of the ברייתא's ruling about long hair. The next step answers this.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק about wine openly mentions death, so that part of the ברייתא is clear. No פסוק openly says this about long hair, so the גמרא asks how it is learned. The source will matter for whether long hair is compared to wine in other ways too.

phrases.english: It makes sense for those who drank wine,
since it is written explicitly about them:
'Drink no wine nor strong drink,'
but those with long hair, from where do we know it?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the source behind part of the ברייתא quoted in step 6
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The scriptural source for the death penalty of a long-haired כהן

steps.title: The source: long hair is placed right next to wine
steps.stepSummary: Two neighboring פסוקים in יחזקאל compare long-haired כהנים to wine-drinkers, so both carry death.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it is written: 'Neither shall they shave their heads, nor let their hair grow long,' and right after that it is written: 'Neither shall any כהן drink wine when they enter the inner courtyard.' So long hair is compared to wine. Just as wine-drinkers are punished by death, long-haired ones are also punished by death.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question from Step 7 by showing where the death penalty for long hair comes from.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק about long hair is followed right away by the פסוק about wine. Because they sit side by side, the גמרא learns one from the other (a היקש). The death penalty that the תורה gives wine-drinkers is therefore applied to long-haired כהנים too.

keyTerms.meaning: They were compared (by placing the two side by side)
Punished by death (at the hands of Heaven)

phrases.english: As it is written: 'Neither shall they shave their heads,'
'nor let their hair grow long,'
and it is written right after it:
'Neither shall any priest drink wine'
'when they enter the inner courtyard,'
so those with long hair are compared to those who drank wine:
just as those who drank wine are punished by death,
so too those with long hair are punished by death.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 7 about the source for the death penalty for long hair.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The source for the death penalty for a long-haired כהן.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The neighboring פסוקים in יחזקאל 44:20-21 compare long hair to wine, so both carry death.

steps.title: Should long hair also invalidate the service?
steps.stepSummary: If long hair is compared to wine, it should also make the עבודה invalid, which would undo רב אשי's distinction.
steps.simpleTranslation: And from this comparison: just as wine-drinkers make the service invalid, long-haired ones should also make the service invalid!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes the comparison further. If long hair is like wine for death, maybe it is also like wine for making the עבודה invalid.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב אשי's answer in Step 5 depends on wine invalidating the עבודה while long hair does not. If the היקש compares them completely, long hair would also invalidate the עבודה. Then רב אשי's reason for a decree on wine but not on hair would fall apart.

keyTerms.meaning: And from it (from this same comparison)

phrases.english: And from this:

phrases.aramaic: אִי מָה שְׁתוּיֵי יַיִן דְּמַחֲלִי עֲבוֹדָה
phrases.english: if just as those who drank wine invalidate the service,
so too those with long hair should invalidate the service!

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמִינַּהּ: אִי מָה שְׁתוּיֵי יַיִן דְּמַחֲלִי עֲבוֹדָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the comparison from Step 8 to attack רב אשי's distinction from Step 5.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב אשי's claim that long hair does not invalidate the עבודה
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If long hair is compared to wine, the comparison should cover every law, including invalidating the עבודה.

steps.title: The comparison covers only death
steps.stepSummary: The היקש compares long hair to wine only for the death penalty, not for invalidating the עבודה.
steps.simpleTranslation: No. When they were compared, it was only for death. For invalidating the service, they were not compared.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the comparison is limited. It teaches only the death penalty.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The גמרא says the היקש was made for one purpose only, the death penalty. Invalidating the עבודה is not carried over from wine to long hair. So רב אשי's distinction still stands.

keyTerms.meaning: For the purpose of invalidating the service

phrases.english: No: when they were compared,
it was for death that they were compared,
but for invalidating the service
they were not compared.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא: כִּי אִיתַּקּוּשׁ — לְמִיתָה הוּא דְּאִתַּקּוּשׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 9.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limits the scope of the היקש
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The comparison to wine covers every law, including invalidating the עבודה.
steps.terutzMaskana: The comparison was made only for the death penalty.

steps.title: Who taught this law before יחזקאל?
steps.stepSummary: רבינא asks how a law found only in יחזקאל could have been known before he came.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבינא said to רב אשי: Before יחזקאל came, who said this law?
steps.whatsHappening: רבינא questions the source itself. The law about long hair seems to begin only with יחזקאל.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A נביא cannot make up a new law. If this law appears only in יחזקאל, we need to know what it rested on before his time. The question puts the whole source from Step 8 in doubt.

phrases.english: Ravina said to Rav Ashi:
This law: before Yechezkel came,
who said it?

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רָבִינָא לְרַב אָשֵׁי: הָא, מִקַּמֵּי דַּאֲתָא יְחֶזְקֵאל, מַאן אַמְרַהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the source from Step 8 because it comes from יחזקאל rather than the תורה.
steps.kashyaTarget: The source from יחזקאל for the long-hair law
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A נביא cannot create new law, so the law must have existed before יחזקאל, yet no earlier source is known.

steps.title: The same question applies to רב חסדא's uncircumcised כהן
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי points out that רב חסדא also learns a law only from יחזקאל, so the same question applies there.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: By your reasoning, what about what רב חסדא said: 'We did not learn this from the תורה of משה; we learned it from the words of tradition: Any stranger, uncircumcised in heart and uncircumcised in flesh, shall not enter My Sanctuary.' Before יחזקאל came, who said that law?
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי answers by turning the question around. רבינא's question would also hit an accepted law of רב חסדא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב חסדא says the law that an uncircumcised כהן may not serve comes only from יחזקאל. If רבינא's question were a real problem, it would be a problem there too. This sets up the shared answer in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: Words of tradition, meaning נביאים and כתובים

phrases.english: He said to him: And according to your reasoning,
what about that which Rav Chisda said:

phrases.aramaic: דָּבָר זֶה מִתּוֹרַת מֹשֶׁה לֹא לָמַדְנוּ,
phrases.english: 'This matter we did not learn from the Torah of Moshe,'
'but we learned it from the words of tradition:'
phrases.notes: He means the books of the נביאים, here the book of יחזקאל.

phrases.english: 'Any stranger, uncircumcised in heart'

phrases.aramaic: וְעֶרֶל בָּשָׂר לֹא יָבוֹא אֶל מִקְדָּשִׁי״
phrases.english: 'and uncircumcised in flesh, shall not enter My Sanctuary.'
phrases.notes: יחזקאל 44:9. רב חסדא uses it to teach that an uncircumcised כהן may not serve.

phrases.english: This law: before Yechezkel came,
who said it?

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: וּלְטַעְמָיךְ, הָא דְּאָמַר רַב חִסְדָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רבינא in Step 11 by showing his question applies equally to רב חסדא's accepted law.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבינא's assumption that a law found only in יחזקאל has no earlier source
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רב חסדא's accepted law about an uncircumcised כהן also comes only from יחזקאל, so the question proves too much.

steps.title: It was an old tradition that יחזקאל attached to a verse
steps.stepSummary: The law was known as an oral tradition, and יחזקאל only gave it a פסוק to lean on.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, they had learned it as a tradition, and יחזקאל came and attached it to a verse.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the answer that works for both laws. יחזקאל did not invent anything; he gave an old oral law a written support.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Before יחזקאל, these laws were already known as part of the oral tradition. יחזקאל's פסוק is a support (אסמכתא), not the origin. That answers the question of who said it before him.

keyTerms.meaning: They had it as a learned oral tradition
He attached it to a פסוק as support

phrases.english: Rather, they had learned it as a tradition,
phrases.notes: The letter in square brackets is the corrected wording, so read it as 'they learned.'

phrases.english: and Yechezkel came and attached it to a verse.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא גְּמָרָא גְּמִירִ[י] לַהּ, וַאֲתָא יְחֶזְקֵאל וְאַסְמְכַהּ אַקְּרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the answer that resolves both רב חסדא's case and רבינא's question.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reframes the פסוק as support for an earlier oral tradition
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The law began with יחזקאל, so it had no earlier source.
steps.terutzMaskana: The law was an old oral tradition, and יחזקאל only attached it to a פסוק.
steps.confusionAlert: יחזקאל is not making a new law here. The law was already known, and he only gave it a פסוק to lean on.

steps.title: The long-hair tradition taught only death, not invalid service
steps.stepSummary: The long-hair law was also an oral tradition, and it included only the death penalty, not invalidating the עבודה.
steps.simpleTranslation: Here too, they had learned it as a tradition, and יחזקאל came and attached it to a verse. When they learned the law, it was for death; for invalidating the service, they did not learn it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא applies the same answer to long hair and closes the topic. The tradition included only the death penalty.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Long hair was also an old oral law that יחזקאל attached to a פסוק. Since we know it from tradition, the tradition decides how far it goes, and it covered only death. This confirms רב אשי from Step 5: long hair does not invalidate the עבודה, so there was no decree.

keyTerms.meaning: The law as received by tradition

steps.whatToRemember: The long-hair law is an old oral tradition, and יחזקאל's פסוק only supports it. The tradition gave only the death penalty, so long hair does not invalidate the עבודה, and רב אשי's distinction stands.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows a key idea: a law in נביאים can be an old oral tradition, and the tradition itself decides how far the law reaches.

phrases.english: Here too:
they had learned it as a tradition,
and Yechezkel came and attached it to a verse;
when they learned the law, it was for death;
for invalidating the service, they did not learn it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies the answer of Step 13 to long hair and limits that tradition to death.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The long-hair law is an oral tradition supported by יחזקאל. It carries death but does not invalidate the עבודה, so רב אשי's distinction holds.

steps.title: The day before a 'no eulogy' day is also forbidden
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה: for a day listed in מגילת תענית as 'no הספד', the day before is forbidden and the day after is allowed.
steps.simpleTranslation: Any day that מגילת תענית marks as 'not to eulogize': the day before it is forbidden, and the day after it is allowed.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new topic by quoting a line from the משנה about the days listed in מגילת תענית. This sets up the discussion that follows.
steps.deeperAnalysis: מגילת תענית is a list of happy days on which fasting, and sometimes הספד, is not allowed. The משנה adds that the ban on הספד also covers the day before, but not the day after.

keyTerms.meaning: An old list of happy days on which fasting or eulogizing is not allowed

phrases.english: Any day about which it is written in מגילת תענית
'not to eulogize'
the day before it is forbidden, the day after it is permitted.
phrases.notes: Forbidden and permitted here mean to eulogize on that day.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic, separate from the wine and long-hair discussion in steps 1-14.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: On a 'no הספד' day in מגילת תענית, the day before is also forbidden; the day after is allowed.

steps.title: The opening of the list in מגילת תענית
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא quotes the start of מגילת תענית: from ראש חודש ניסן to the eighth, and from the eighth to the end of פסח, הספד is not allowed.
steps.simpleTranslation: These are the days when we do not fast, and on some of them we also do not eulogize. From ראש חודש ניסן until the eighth of the month, the daily offering was set up, so no eulogizing on those days. From the eighth until the end of the festival, the festival of שבועות was restored, so no eulogizing on those days.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings the actual words of מגילת תענית so it can study them next. This is setup for the question that follows.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The list gives two stretches of days in ניסן, each tied to a happy event from history. Both stretches are marked 'no הספד', which is stricter than just 'no fasting'.

keyTerms.meaning: The start of the month, ראש חודש

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
These are the days on which one may not fast,
and on some of them one may not eulogize:

phrases.aramaic: מֵרֵישׁ יַרְחָא דְנִיסָן וְעַד תְּמָנְיָא בֵּיהּ
phrases.english: From the start of the month of ניסן until the eighth of it,
the daily offering was established, so one may not eulogize on them.
From the eighth of it until the end of the festival,

phrases.aramaic: אִיתּוֹתַב חַגָּא דְשָׁבוּעַיָּא, דְּלָא לְמִיסְפַּד בְּהוֹן.
phrases.english: the festival of שבועות was restored, so one may not eulogize on them.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: אִלֵּין יוֹמַיָּא דְּלָא לְהִתְעַנָּאָה בְּהוֹן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings the actual text of מגילת תענית that the משנה in step 15 was talking about.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: From ראש חודש ניסן through the end of פסח, fasting and הספד are not allowed.

steps.title: Why start the list from ראש חודש?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why מגילת תענית starts from ראש חודש ניסן, since ראש חודש is already a festive day when הספד is forbidden.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Master said: From ראש חודש ניסן until the eighth, the daily offering was set up, so no eulogizing. Why do I need it to say from ראש חודש? Let it say from the second of ניסן, since ראש חודש itself is a festive day and it is already forbidden!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא repeats a line from the list and asks why it needed to include ראש חודש at all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: ראש חודש is already a festive day on which הספד is not allowed. So listing it in מגילת תענית seems to add nothing, and the list could have started from the second of ניסן.

phrases.english: The Master said:

phrases.aramaic: מֵרֵישׁ יַרְחָא דְנִיסָן עַד תְּמָנְיָא בֵּיהּ
phrases.english: From the start of the month of ניסן until the eighth of it,
the daily offering was established, so one may not eulogize.
Why do I need 'from the start of the month'?
Let it say 'from the second of ניסן',

phrases.aramaic: וְרֹאשׁ חוֹדֶשׁ גּוּפֵיהּ יוֹם טוֹב הוּא וְאָסוּר!
phrases.english: since ראש חודש itself is a festive day and is forbidden anyway!

steps.triggerLanguage: לְמָה לִי מֵרֵישׁ יַרְחָא? לֵימָא מִתְּרֵי בְּנִיסָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the wording of the list quoted in step 16.
steps.kashyaTarget: The words 'from ראש חודש ניסן' in מגילת תענית
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: ראש חודש is already forbidden for הספד, so including it in the list seems pointless.

steps.title: רב: listing it forbids the day before
steps.stepSummary: רב answers that ראש חודש is listed only to forbid the day before it.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב said: It was only needed to forbid the day before it.
steps.whatsHappening: רב explains why the list includes ראש חודש.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since a day in מגילת תענית also forbids the day before it (step 15), listing ראש חודש ניסן makes the last day of אדר forbidden too. So the listing does add something.

phrases.english: רב said:

phrases.aramaic: לֹא נִצְרְכָה אֶלָּא לֶאֱסוֹר יוֹם שֶׁלְּפָנָיו.
phrases.english: It was needed only to forbid the day before it.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב: לֹא נִצְרְכָה אֶלָּא לֶאֱסוֹר יוֹם שֶׁלְּפָנָיו
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 17.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Finds a new purpose for the wording
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Listing ראש חודש adds nothing because it is already forbidden.
steps.terutzMaskana: Listing it makes the day before ראש חודש ניסן forbidden, using the rule of step 15.

steps.title: The day before ראש חודש should be forbidden anyway
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks that the day before is already forbidden simply because it is the day before ראש חודש.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the day before as well: derive it from the fact that it is the day before ראש חודש!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on רב's answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If a festive day forbids the day before it, then ראש חודש itself should forbid the day before it. So the list still seems to add nothing.

keyTerms.meaning: Let him derive it from (another reason)

phrases.english: And the day before as well,
derive it from the fact that it is
the day before ראש חודש!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב's answer in step 18.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב's claim that the listing is needed to forbid the day before
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The day before ראש חודש should already be forbidden because ראש חודש itself would forbid it.

steps.title: A Torah festival needs no extra fence
steps.stepSummary: ראש חודש is from the תורה, and תורה laws do not need the extra protection of forbidding the day before.
steps.simpleTranslation: ראש חודש is from the תורה, and a תורה law does not need reinforcing.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that ראש חודש by itself does not forbid the day before it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Forbidding the day before is an extra fence to strengthen a law. תורה laws like ראש חודש are strong enough on their own, so only the listing in מגילת תענית forbids the day before ראש חודש ניסן. That is why רב's answer works.

phrases.english: ראש חודש is from the Torah,
and a Torah law does not need reinforcement.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 19 and saves רב's answer.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Draws a line between Torah law and rabbinic law
steps.terutzHavaAmina: ראש חודש by itself forbids the day before, so the listing is not needed.
steps.terutzMaskana: Torah festivals do not forbid the day before; only rabbinic days do, so the listing is needed.

steps.title: A ברייתא: rabbinic days need a fence, Torah days do not
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא says that days in מגילת תענית forbid the days before and after, but שבת and יום טוב do not, because תורה laws need no reinforcement and rabbinic laws do.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it is taught: These days written in מגילת תענית, the days before and after them are forbidden. שבתות and ימים טובים are themselves forbidden, but the days before and after them are allowed. What is the difference between them? These are תורה laws, and תורה laws do not need reinforcement. Those are rabbinic laws, and rabbinic laws need reinforcement.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that supports the answer in step 20.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא states the exact rule the גמרא used: תורה days like שבת and יום טוב stand on their own, while rabbinic days like those in מגילת תענית get a fence around them. This backs up the claim that ראש חודש, a תורה day, does not forbid the day before by itself.
steps.whatToRemember: תורה festivals (שבת, יום טוב, ראש חודש) do not forbid fasting on the day before or after. Rabbinic days in מגילת תענית do, because rabbinic laws need a protective fence.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't assume this ברייתא matches the משנה in step 15 exactly: the משנה allowed the day after, while the ברייתא says the days before and after are forbidden. The גמרא brings the ברייתא here only for its contrast between Torah days and rabbinic days.
steps.whyThisMatters: The rule 'rabbinic laws need reinforcement, תורה laws do not' explains why rabbinic days get extra protection.

phrases.english: As it is taught:
These days that are written in מגילת תענית:
the days before them and after them are forbidden,
phrases.notes: Here this means forbidden to fast.

phrases.english: שבתות and ימים טובים: they themselves are forbidden,
but the days before them and after them are permitted.
And what is the difference between this and that?
These are Torah laws,
and Torah laws do not need reinforcement,
those are rabbinic laws,
and rabbinic laws need reinforcement.

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּתַנְיָא: הַיָּמִים הָאֵלֶּה הַכְּתוּבִין בִּמְגִילַּת תַּעֲנִית
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a ברייתא to support the answer of step 20.
steps.raayaObject: The rule that Torah laws do not need reinforcement
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא contrasting the days of מגילת תענית with שבת and יום טוב

steps.title: Quoting another line from מגילת תענית
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes a line from מגילת תענית: from the eighth of ניסן until the end of פסח, הספד is forbidden because the date of שבועות was restored.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Master said: From the eighth of ניסן until the end of the festival of פסח, the correct date of שבועות was restored, so it was decreed that people may not eulogize.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back and quotes a new line from מגילת תענית. It is setting up a question about the wording.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is a different date range from the ראש חודש ניסן line discussed before. The days from the eighth of ניסן through the end of פסח became days of celebration, so הספד on them was forbidden. The key words to watch are 'until the end of the festival.'

keyTerms.meaning: The festival. Here it means פסח.
Was restored, or was set up again.
To eulogize, to say a הספד.

phrases.english: The Master said:
From the eighth of it until the end of the festival
phrases.notes: 'Of it' means of the month of ניסן, and 'the festival' is פסח.

phrases.english: the festival of שבועות was restored,
that one may not eulogize.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר מָר: מִתְּמָנְיָא בֵּיהּ עַד סוֹף מוֹעֲדָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the ראש חודש ניסן line to a new line of מגילת תענית that has a similar wording problem.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: From the eighth of ניסן through the end of פסח, הספד is forbidden.

steps.title: Why say 'until the end of the festival'?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the text says 'until the end of the festival' when it could just say 'until the festival,' since פסח itself is already a יום טוב when הספד is forbidden.
steps.simpleTranslation: Why do I need 'until the end of the festival'? Let it say 'until the festival,' because the festival itself is a יום טוב and הספד is already forbidden on it!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the wording. It points out that including the days of פסח seems to add nothing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The days of פסח are already forbidden for הספד because they are a יום טוב. So מגילת תענית only needed to cover the days before פסח, the eighth through the fourteenth. This is the same kind of question the גמרא asked about ראש חודש in step 17.

keyTerms.meaning: 'Why do I need it?' The גמרא is asking why some words are there if they seem unnecessary.
Let it say. The גמרא suggests shorter wording.
A festival day, when הספד is forbidden.

phrases.english: Why do I need 'until the end of the festival'?
Let it say 'until the festival,'

phrases.aramaic: וּמוֹעֵד גּוּפֵיהּ יוֹם טוֹב הוּא וְאָסוּר!
phrases.english: and the festival itself is a יום טוב, and it is forbidden!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the wording of the line quoted in step 22.
steps.kashyaTarget: The words 'until the end of the festival' in מגילת תענית.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: פסח is a יום טוב, so הספד on it is already forbidden by its own status. Listing those days in מגילת תענית seems to add nothing.

steps.title: רב פפא answers using רב's approach
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא begins to answer that this wording should be explained the way רב explained the listing of ראש חודש: it is needed for a specific purpose.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said: Explain it the way רב did: it is needed only... (the answer continues on the next amud).
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא starts to answer by using the same approach רב used for ראש חודש ניסן. His full answer continues on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 18, רב said ראש חודש was listed only to forbid a day next to it. רב פפא says the same kind of reasoning explains why the days of פסח are listed here. So the extra words are not useless; they serve some other purpose that he is about to state.

keyTerms.meaning: As רב said. He is using an explanation that was already given.
It is needed only for... The opening of an answer that shows what the words are really for.

steps.confusionAlert: The sentence is cut off here. The part that says exactly which day is being forbidden comes on the next amud, so do not fill it in from step 18.

phrases.english: רב פפא said:
As רב said:
phrases.notes: This is רב's answer about ראש חודש from step 18. רב פפא uses it again here.

phrases.english: It is needed only...

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב פָּפָּא: כִּדְאָמַר רַב — לֹא נִצְרְכָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 23 by using רב's principle from step 18.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Applying an earlier principle: the extra wording is there for a specific purpose.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Listing the days of פסח seemed pointless, since they are already a יום טוב.
steps.terutzMaskana: Following רב's approach, the listing is needed for a specific purpose, which רב פפא states on the next amud.
